title: Vector Databases and Semantic Search
subtitle: Build semantic search that's fast and measurably right: embeddings, exact and approximate indexes, compression, hybrid ranking, filtering and vector databases.
outcomes: Choose an embedding model and similarity measure for search, and explain why normalised vectors make cosine, inner product and L2 rankings agree
Build exact, IVF and HNSW indexes and tune nprobe, M and efSearch against recall@k on held-out queries
Compress vectors with scalar, binary and product quantisation, and recover accuracy by re-ranking
Fuse BM25 with dense retrieval, tune it on dev queries and report recall@k, MRR and nDCG with a bootstrap interval
Filter vector search without losing results, and choose between FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus for a workload
prerequisites: Python and NumPy at the level of Python Foundations for Data Science, and Machine Learning Foundations with Python; Text Representation: From Vectors to Context helps. You need Python 3.10 or later with numpy, pandas, scikit-learn, faiss-cpu and sentence-transformers (one 90 MB model download), and Docker for the last lab.
description:
Semantic search finds what people mean rather than the words they typed, and it's the retrieval layer under most AI assistants. This course takes you inside it. You'll embed text with a pretrained model and see why normalised vectors make cosine, inner product and Euclidean distance agree; build exact search in NumPy and keep its answers as ground truth; build an inverted-file index from scratch and tune FAISS IVF and HNSW indexes on recall, latency and memory; and compress vectors with int8, binary and product quantisation, winning accuracy back by re-ranking.

Then you'll make search good and safe to use: evaluate relevance with graded queries, recall@k, MRR and nDCG, and a bootstrap that says whether a gain is real; fuse BM25 with dense retrieval; filter by tenant without losing results; and run it all in PostgreSQL with pgvector, with a clear-eyed comparison of FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus. Every lab runs on a laptop and was run end to end, and the checks quote its real output. The course stops at retrieval: Building RAG and Agentic Systems takes it on to generation and agents.

modules.title: Embeddings and similarity for search
modules.summary: How embedding models turn text into vectors for retrieval, which similarity measure to use, and what exact nearest-neighbour search costs: the ground truth for everything that follows.

lessons.title: Embedding models for retrieval
objectives: Explain how a bi-encoder embedding model supports search
Choose an embedding model and its settings for a retrieval task
key_points: A bi-encoder embedding model maps a text to one fixed-length vector. Trained contrastively on pairs such as a question and the passage that answers it, it places related texts close together, so search becomes finding the vectors nearest the query's.

Documents are embedded once, ahead of time, and only the query at search time. The same model, version and pre-processing must embed both: vectors from different models aren't comparable, even when they have the same number of dimensions.

Symmetric search compares texts of the same kind, such as duplicate questions; asymmetric search matches a short query to a longer passage. Pick a model trained for your case, and add any prefixes it expects, such as 'query: ' and 'passage: ' for the E5 family.

Transformer encoders produce a vector per token and pool them, often by averaging, into one. Input past the model's maximum length is cut off silently (256 tokens for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 in sentence-transformers), so split long documents into chunks before embedding them.

More dimensions can hold more detail but cost memory and time per comparison. Some models are trained so that their first dimensions work on their own (Matryoshka representation learning), so vectors can be truncated and re-normalised, once you've measured the loss.
Store the model's name and version with every vector. Changing the model means re-embedding the whole collection into a new index, never mixing old and new vectors in one.

lessons.title: Similarity measures and normalisation
objectives: Calculate the dot product, cosine similarity and Euclidean distance of two vectors
Explain when the three measures rank neighbours identically and when they don't
key_points: The dot product q·x sums the products of matching coordinates; cosine similarity divides it by both vectors' lengths, so it depends only on the angle between them; Euclidean (L2) distance is the length of q − x.

For vectors of length 1, ||q − x||² = 2 − 2·cos(q, x), so L2 distance, cosine similarity and the inner product all rank neighbours identically. Normalise once, at index time, and use the inner product, the cheapest of the three to compute.

On raw, unnormalised vectors the measures disagree: the inner product favours long vectors whatever their direction. Maximum inner product search suits models trained for it, such as recommenders whose vector length carries meaning; otherwise use the model's training measure.

Similarity scores aren't calibrated probabilities: a cosine of 0.5 can be a strong match for one model and a weak one for another. Set any score threshold per model on labelled examples, and rely on ranks where you can.

In high dimensions, distances between random points bunch together, so the nearest and farthest points end up almost equally far away. Real embeddings have structure, with topics forming clusters, which makes nearest neighbours meaningful and approximate search possible.

lessons.title: Exact nearest-neighbour search and its cost
objectives: Implement brute-force k-nearest-neighbour search with matrix multiplication
Estimate the memory and compute an exact index needs
key_points: Exact (flat) k-nearest-neighbour search scores the query against every vector, N × d multiply-adds per query, and keeps the best k. Its answers are perfect, and they're the ground truth that every approximate index is measured against.

Batch the queries: one matrix multiplication of the query matrix by the transposed collection scores many queries at once in optimised BLAS code. For L2, expand ||q − x||² = ||q||² − 2q·x + ||x||² and compute the ||x||² terms once.
Select the top k with a partial sort, such as numpy.argpartition followed by sorting only those k: about O(N) work per query instead of O(N log N) for a full sort.
Memory is N × d × 4 bytes in float32: a million 768-dimensional vectors need about 3.1 GB before any index overhead, which is often what decides that exact search no longer fits on one machine.

Exact search is the right choice for small collections, for filters that leave few candidates and for building evaluation ground truth. Keep an ID array beside the matrix so that row numbers map back to documents.

"""Make the course's synthetic embedding collection: 50,000 vectors in topic clusters, 500 held-out queries
from the same distribution, and a tenant label on every vector for the filtering labs. Fixed seed: everyone
gets identical files."""
import argparse
import pathlib

import numpy as np

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=50_000)
p.add_argument("--dim", type=int, default=64)
p.add_argument("--topics", type=int, default=100)
p.add_argument("--queries", type=int, default=500)
p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=7)
a = p.parse_args()

rng = np.random.default_rng(a.seed)
centres = rng.normal(size=(a.topics, a.dim)) * 0.6       # topic centres, overlapping as real topics do
spread = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.0, size=a.topics)             # some topics tight, some loose
weights = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(a.topics) * 2.0)          # some topics much more common than others


def sample(m):
    topic = rng.choice(a.topics, size=m, p=weights)
    x = centres[topic] + rng.normal(size=(m, a.dim)) * spread[topic, None]
    x *= rng.lognormal(0.0, 0.25, size=(m, 1))            # raw model outputs vary in length
    return x.astype(np.float32)


base = sample(a.n)
queries = sample(a.queries)
share = [0.40, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05, 0.03, 0.015, 0.005]  # tenants 0-7, from big to tiny
tenant = rng.choice(len(share), size=a.n, p=share).astype(np.int16)

out = pathlib.Path("data")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
np.save(out / "base.npy", base)
np.save(out / "queries.npy", queries)
np.save(out / "tenant.npy", tenant)
print(f"wrote data/base.npy {base.shape} {base.dtype}, data/queries.npy {queries.shape}, data/tenant.npy")
print("tenant shares:", " ".join(f"{t}:{np.mean(tenant == t):.3f}" for t in range(len(share))))

"""Module 1 lab: exact k-NN search with NumPy, and what normalisation does to the metrics."""
import time

import numpy as np

from vecs import exact_search, recall_at_k, top_k, unit

base, queries = np.load("data/base.npy"), np.load("data/queries.npy")
print(f"collection: {base.shape[0]} vectors x {base.shape[1]} dims, {base.dtype}, {base.nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB")
norms = np.linalg.norm(base, axis=1)
print(f"raw lengths: min {norms.min():.2f}, median {np.median(norms):.2f}, max {norms.max():.2f}")

k = 10
bn, qn = unit(base), unit(queries)
cos = exact_search(qn, bn, k, "ip")
same = np.mean(np.all(cos == exact_search(qn, bn, k, "l2"), axis=1))
print(f"cosine vs L2 on unit vectors: identical top-{k} for {same:.1%} of queries")
print(f"cosine vs raw inner product: overlap@{k} {recall_at_k(exact_search(queries, base, k, 'ip'), cos, k):.3f}")
print(f"cosine vs raw L2:            overlap@{k} {recall_at_k(exact_search(queries, base, k, 'l2'), cos, k):.3f}")

a, b = bn[:1000].astype(np.float64), bn[1000:2000].astype(np.float64)
gap = np.abs(((a - b) ** 2).sum(1) - (2 - 2 * (a * b).sum(1))).max()
print(f"largest gap between ||a-b||^2 and 2 - 2cos(a,b) over 1000 pairs: {gap:.1e}")

scores = qn[:256] @ bn.T                                  # one batch of queries
t_sort = t_part = float("inf")
for _ in range(3):                                        # best of three, to steady the timings
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    full = np.argsort(-scores, axis=1)[:, :k]
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    part = top_k(scores, k)
    t_sort, t_part = min(t_sort, t1 - t0), min(t_part, time.perf_counter() - t1)
print(f"argpartition gives the same top-{k} as a full sort: {bool(np.all(full == part))} "
      f"(sort {1e3 * t_sort:.0f} ms, argpartition {1e3 * t_part:.0f} ms for 256 queries)")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
gt = exact_search(qn, bn, 100, "ip")
dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"exact top-100 for {len(qn)} queries: {dt:.2f} s, {1e3 * dt / len(qn):.2f} ms per query")
np.save("data/gt.npy", gt)
print("saved data/gt.npy: the ground truth for every later lab")
for n, d in [(1_000_000, 384), (1_000_000, 768), (10_000_000, 768)]:
    print(f"flat float32 index for {n:,} x {d}: {n * d * 4 / 1e9:.2f} GB")

"""Module 1 lab, part 2: real sentence embeddings from a small open model (downloads about 90 MB once)."""
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

docs = [
    "How to reset your password if you are locked out of your account",
    "Setting up the VPN client on a new laptop",
    "Requesting annual leave and checking your remaining holiday allowance",
    "The printer on the third floor reports a paper jam",
    "Claiming travel expenses after a business trip",
    "Turning on two-factor authentication for your email",
]
queries = ["I can't remember my login details", "how many days off do I have left", "printer stuck"]

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
D = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)
Q = model.encode(queries, normalize_embeddings=True)
print(f"{D.shape[1]} dimensions, lengths {np.linalg.norm(D, axis=1).min():.3f} to {np.linalg.norm(D, axis=1).max():.3f}, "
      f"inputs truncated after {model.max_seq_length} tokens")
for q, row in zip(queries, Q @ D.T):
    best = np.argsort(-row)[:2]
    shared = set(q.lower().split()) & set(docs[best[0]].lower().split())
    print(f"{q!r}: {row[best[0]]:.3f} {docs[best[0]]!r} (shared words: {', '.join(sorted(shared)) or 'none'}); "
          f"next {row[best[1]]:.3f}")

hints: sentence-transformers needs PyTorch. On Linux, pip installs a GPU build with large extra libraries by default; install the CPU-only build first with pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu to save several gigabytes.
If embed_demo.py can't download the model, check your connection or proxy settings. After the first run it loads from the cache; set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 to stop it checking for updates.
Timings depend on your computer; the overlaps and counts shouldn't. A different NumPy version can change a last digit.
A cosine of 0.556 may look low, but scores are only comparable within one model: what matters is that the right article is first and well ahead of the next (0.232).

modules.title: Approximate nearest neighbours: IVF and HNSW
modules.summary: Why approximate search, how to measure it against exact search, and how inverted-file indexes and HNSW graphs trade recall for speed and memory.

lessons.title: Measuring approximate search
objectives: Define recall@k for an approximate index
Compare indexes fairly on recall, latency, memory and build time
key_points: An approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) index examines only part of the collection, so it returns most, not all, of the true neighbours. Its recall@k is the share of the exact top k it returns, averaged over queries: 0.95 means 19 of every 20 true neighbours were found.

Four quantities trade against each other: recall, query latency or throughput, memory, and build or update time. Every index has knobs that move it along that curve, so compare indexes at the same recall, not at their default settings.
Benchmark with held-out queries like production's, at the k you actually serve, and report latency percentiles from many single queries; the throughput of large batches is a different measurement.

ANN recall measures agreement with exact search, not relevance. A perfect index over a poor embedding model still returns poor results, so judge the model with relevance labels and the index against exact search.
Tune the knobs on one query set and confirm on another, and measure again as the collection grows or changes: a setting that gave 0.95 recall on a small collection can give less on a larger one.

lessons.title: Inverted-file (IVF) indexes
objectives: Explain how an IVF index partitions vectors and searches nprobe lists
Choose nlist and nprobe from measurements
key_points: An IVF index runs k-means to find nlist centroids, which divide the space into cells, and stores each vector in the inverted list of its nearest centroid. A query is compared with the centroids, and only the vectors in the nprobe nearest lists are scored.

Each query scores the nlist centroids plus about nprobe × N / nlist vectors. Raising nprobe finds neighbours just across cell boundaries, raising recall and cost, and nprobe = nlist scans everything, which gives exact results.

For the same nprobe, more lists means shorter lists and less work but lower recall, so compare list counts by the work needed to reach a target recall. FAISS's guidelines suggest an nlist between about 4√N and 16√N.

Train k-means on a sample that represents the data, with enough points per centroid (FAISS warns below 39). Popular topics make some lists much longer than others, and queries that probe them are slower.

Adding a vector only means assigning it to its nearest centroid, and deleting one means removing it from a list; but if the data drifts away from the training sample, the lists become unbalanced and the index needs retraining.

lessons.title: HNSW graphs
objectives: Describe how HNSW builds and searches a layered graph
Tune M, efConstruction and efSearch, and estimate HNSW's memory
key_points: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World, from Malkov and Yashunin) links every vector to approximate nearest neighbours in a graph. Each vector also appears on higher, sparser layers with exponentially falling probability, about 1/M of them on layer 1, which act as express lanes.

A search enters at the top layer, moves greedily towards the query and drops a layer at a time. On the bottom layer it runs a best-first search that keeps a candidate list of size efSearch, and returns the best k from it.

M sets the links per vector (FAISS keeps 2M on the bottom layer), so a higher M raises recall and memory. efConstruction sets how widely insertion looks for neighbours: a better graph for a longer build. efSearch is the query-time knob.

Links cost memory on top of the vectors: with 4-byte neighbour IDs, about 8 × M bytes per vector on the bottom layer. In the lab, M = 16 added 144 bytes per vector, more than half the size of a 64-dimensional float32 vector.

HNSW gives high recall at low latency and accepts inserts without training, but it builds more slowly than IVF, the graph normally lives in RAM, and deleted vectors are usually marked and skipped until a rebuild.

"""Module 2 lab: an inverted-file (IVF) index from scratch with k-means and NumPy."""
import time

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

from vecs import load, recall_at_k, top_k

base, queries = load()
gt = np.load("data/gt.npy")
nlist, k = 256, 10

t0 = time.perf_counter()
sample = base[np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(base), 20_000, replace=False)]   # train on a sample
km = KMeans(n_clusters=nlist, n_init=1, max_iter=25, random_state=0).fit(sample)
centroids = km.cluster_centers_ / np.linalg.norm(km.cluster_centers_, axis=1, keepdims=True)
centroids = centroids.astype(np.float32)
assign = np.argmax(base @ centroids.T, axis=1)            # each vector joins its nearest centroid's list
lists = [np.flatnonzero(assign == c) for c in range(nlist)]
sizes = np.array([len(ids) for ids in lists])
print(f"trained {nlist} lists in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; vectors per list: min {sizes.min()}, "
      f"median {int(np.median(sizes))}, max {sizes.max()}")


def search(q, nprobe):
    """Compare q with the centroids, then scan only the vectors in the nprobe nearest lists."""
    cells = top_k((centroids @ q)[None, :], nprobe)[0]
    ids = np.concatenate([lists[c] for c in cells])
    best = top_k((base[ids] @ q)[None, :], k)[0]
    return ids[best], len(ids)


for nprobe in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, nlist]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    results = [search(q, nprobe) for q in queries]
    ms = 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(queries)
    found = np.array([ids for ids, _ in results])
    scanned = np.mean([n for _, n in results]) / len(base)
    print(f"nprobe={nprobe:>3}: recall@10 {recall_at_k(found, gt, k):.3f}, scanned {scanned:6.1%} of the "
          f"vectors, {ms:.2f} ms/query")

"""Module 2 lab, part 2: the same trade-offs with FAISS: IVF with two list counts, and HNSW graphs."""
import time

import faiss
import numpy as np

from vecs import load, recall_at_k

faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1)          # one thread: reproducible builds and honest per-query latency
base, queries = load()
gt = np.load("data/gt.npy")
n, d = base.shape
k = 10


def mb(index):
    return faiss.serialize_index(index).nbytes / 1e6


def sweep(index, label, knob, values, apply):
    for v in values:
        apply(v)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        _, found = index.search(queries, k)
        ms = 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(queries)
        print(f"  {label} {knob}={v:<4} recall@10 {recall_at_k(found, gt, k):.3f}  {ms:.3f} ms/query")


flat = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)
flat.add(base)
print(f"Flat: {mb(flat):.1f} MB, recall@10 1.000 by definition")

for nlist in (256, 1024):
    ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), d, nlist, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ivf.train(base)
    ivf.add(base)
    print(f"IVF{nlist},Flat: built in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s, {mb(ivf):.1f} MB")
    sweep(ivf, f"IVF{nlist}", "nprobe", [1, 4, 16, 64], lambda v: setattr(ivf, "nprobe", v))

for m in (16, 32):
    hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, m, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
    hnsw.hnsw.efConstruction = 80
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    hnsw.add(base)
    print(f"HNSW{m},Flat: built in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s, {mb(hnsw):.1f} MB, "
          f"{(mb(hnsw) - mb(flat)) * 1e6 / n:.0f} bytes of links per vector")
    sweep(hnsw, f"HNSW{m}", "efSearch", [16, 32, 64, 128], lambda v: setattr(hnsw.hnsw, "efSearch", v))

hints: If pip can't find a faiss-cpu wheel for your platform, conda install -c pytorch faiss-cpu is the project's own installation route.

The scripts run FAISS on one thread so that builds are reproducible and latencies are per query. Remove faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1) to see multi-threaded speed; HNSW builds then vary slightly between runs.

Latencies depend on your machine; recall should match the checks. The from-scratch index is slower than FAISS because it loops in Python and copies candidate vectors: compare the share of vectors scanned, not its milliseconds.
At 50 million vectors, think about the training sample, list counts from the √N guideline, the memory for HNSW's links and the time to rebuild.

modules.title: Compressing vectors: scalar, binary and product quantisation
modules.summary: Fit more vectors into memory with float16, int8 and binary codes and with product quantisation, and win back accuracy with IVF residuals and re-ranking.

lessons.title: Memory budgets and scalar quantisation
objectives: Work out the memory a vector index needs per vector
Compare float16, int8 and binary quantisation
key_points: An in-memory index needs the vectors plus its own structures: 50,000 float32 vectors of 64 dimensions take 12.8 MB, IVF adds an 8-byte ID per vector and HNSW its links. Work it out per vector before choosing an index or hardware.
Storing vectors as float16 halves their memory with almost no effect on ranking for typical embeddings: the module's lab measured recall@10 of 0.999 against float32.

Int8 scalar quantisation maps each dimension's range onto the 256 values of a byte, with a scale and offset per dimension, using a quarter of float32's memory; the lab's SQ8 index kept recall@10 at 0.981.

Binary quantisation keeps only the sign of each value, one bit per dimension, 32 times smaller than float32, and compares codes by Hamming distance with XOR and a bit count. It loses the most information and suits high-dimensional models with re-scoring.

Over-fetch and re-score: search the compressed codes for more candidates than you need, such as 100 for a top 10, then re-rank them with full-precision vectors, which can live on disk or in cheaper storage.

lessons.title: Product quantisation
objectives: Explain how product quantisation encodes vectors and scores them
Estimate a product-quantised index's size and accuracy
key_points: Product quantisation (Jégou, Douze and Schmid, 2011) splits each vector into m sub-vectors and learns a k-means codebook of 256 centroids for each sub-space, so a vector is stored as m one-byte codes: 256 bytes of float32 become 8 bytes with m = 8.

Asymmetric distance computation keeps the query exact: for each sub-space it scores the query's sub-vector against all 256 centroids once, an m × 256 table, and each stored vector's score is then the sum of m table look-ups, with no decompression.

More sub-vectors means more bytes and a finer approximation: in the lab, recall@10 rose from 0.266 with 8 bytes per vector to 0.504 with 16. Because the scores are approximate, the order near the top shuffles, which is why re-ranking matters.

IVF-PQ combines the two: IVF chooses the cells to scan, and PQ encodes each vector's residual, its difference from its cell's centroid, which varies less than the vector itself and so quantises more accurately.

Codebooks need representative training data: thousands of vectors, since each sub-space has 256 centroids. Sub-spaces should carry similar variance, and OPQ learns a rotation before quantising to balance them.

lessons.title: Re-ranking and choosing a compression scheme
objectives: Design a two-stage search that re-ranks compressed candidates
Choose a compression scheme from a memory budget and a recall target
key_points: A two-stage search retrieves candidates using compressed codes and re-scores them exactly. Its recall@10 equals the share of the true top 10 among the candidates: re-ranking 100 PQ candidates lifted the lab's recall@10 from 0.260 to 0.765.

Re-ranking needs the full vectors somewhere. FAISS's IndexRefineFlat keeps them in RAM (about 275 bytes per vector in the lab), while disk-based designs such as DiskANN keep compressed codes in memory and the full vectors on SSD.

Start from the budget: bytes per vector times the number of vectors, with headroom for growth. Choose the least compression that fits, then measure recall: there's no point in PQ when float16 or int8 already fits.
Reducing dimensions, with PCA or Matryoshka truncation, is another form of compression and combines with quantisation; measure its effect on both ANN recall and end-to-end relevance.
Normalise before quantising when you search by cosine, and quantise with the metric the index uses. Keep the codebooks and settings with the index: codes mean nothing without them.

"""Module 3 lab: product quantisation from scratch, with scalar and binary quantisation for comparison.
Every result is measured against the exact ground truth from module 1."""
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

from vecs import load, recall_at_k, top_k

base, queries = load()
gt = np.load("data/gt.npy")
n, d = base.shape
m, k = 8, 10                       # 8 sub-vectors of 8 dimensions, 256 centroids (one byte) each
ds = d // m
train = base[np.random.default_rng(0).choice(n, 20_000, replace=False)]


def rerank(candidates, k=10):
    """Re-score each query's candidates with the full float32 vectors and keep the best k."""
    return np.array([c[np.argsort(-(base[c] @ q))[:k]] for c, q in zip(candidates, queries)])


# 1. Train a 256-centroid codebook for each sub-space and encode every vector as 8 one-byte codes.
books = np.stack([KMeans(256, n_init=1, max_iter=20, random_state=j).fit(train[:, j * ds:(j + 1) * ds])
                  .cluster_centers_ for j in range(m)]).astype(np.float32)          # shape (8, 256, 8)
codes = np.empty((n, m), dtype=np.uint8)
for j in range(m):
    sub = base[:, j * ds:(j + 1) * ds]
    dist = (sub ** 2).sum(1)[:, None] - 2 * sub @ books[j].T + (books[j] ** 2).sum(1)[None, :]
    codes[:, j] = np.argmin(dist, axis=1)
print(f"PQ 8x8: {codes.nbytes // n} bytes per vector instead of {base.nbytes // n} "
      f"({base.nbytes // codes.nbytes}x smaller), plus {books.nbytes / 1e3:.0f} KB of codebooks")
recon = np.concatenate([books[j][codes[:, j]] for j in range(m)], axis=1)
print(f"mean squared reconstruction error: {np.mean(((base - recon) ** 2).sum(1)):.3f} (each vector has length 1)")


# 2. Asymmetric distance computation: the query stays exact; one 8 x 256 table, then 8 look-ups per vector.
def adc_scores(q):
    table = np.einsum("jcs,js->jc", books, q.reshape(m, ds))      # q's sub-vector . every centroid
    return table[np.arange(m), codes].sum(axis=1)                # approximate inner product with every vector


pq_top = np.stack([top_k(adc_scores(q)[None, :], 100)[0] for q in queries])
print(f"PQ alone:                     recall@10 {recall_at_k(pq_top, gt):.3f}")
print(f"PQ top 100, re-ranked exactly: recall@10 {recall_at_k(rerank(pq_top), gt):.3f}")

# 3. Scalar quantisation: each dimension's range mapped onto 0-255.
lo, hi = base.min(axis=0), base.max(axis=0)
scale = (hi - lo) / 255
sq8 = np.round((base - lo) / scale).astype(np.uint8)
decoded = sq8 * scale + lo
print(f"SQ8 ({sq8.nbytes // n} bytes):              recall@10 {recall_at_k(top_k(queries @ decoded.T, k), gt):.3f}")

# 4. Binary quantisation: one sign bit per dimension, compared by Hamming distance.
bits, qbits = np.packbits(base > 0, axis=1), np.packbits(queries > 0, axis=1)


def hamming(b, q):
    x = b ^ q
    return np.bitwise_count(x).sum(1) if hasattr(np, "bitwise_count") else np.unpackbits(x, axis=1).sum(1)


bin_top = np.stack([top_k(-hamming(bits, qb)[None, :].astype(np.float32), 100)[0] for qb in qbits])
print(f"binary ({bits.nbytes // n} bytes):            recall@10 {recall_at_k(bin_top, gt):.3f}, "
      f"top 100 re-ranked {recall_at_k(rerank(bin_top), gt):.3f}")

"""Module 3 lab, part 2: memory against recall for FAISS's compressed indexes, built with index_factory."""
import time

import faiss
import numpy as np

from vecs import load, recall_at_k

faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1)
base, queries = load()
gt = np.load("data/gt.npy")
n, d = base.shape
params = faiss.ParameterSpace()

print(f"{'index':<20}{'bytes/vector':>13}{'recall@10':>11}{'ms/query':>10}")
for spec in ["Flat", "SQfp16", "SQ8", "PQ8", "PQ16", "IVF256,PQ8", "IVF256,PQ16", "IVF256,PQ8,RFlat"]:
    index = faiss.index_factory(d, spec, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
    index.train(base)
    index.add(base)
    if "IVF" in spec:
        params.set_index_parameters(index, "nprobe=16")
    if "RFlat" in spec:
        faiss.downcast_index(index).k_factor = 10              # re-rank 10 x k candidates exactly
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    _, found = index.search(queries, 10)
    ms = 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(queries)
    size = faiss.serialize_index(index).nbytes / n
    print(f"{spec:<20}{size:>13.1f}{recall_at_k(found, gt):>11.3f}{ms:>10.3f}")

hints: np.bitwise_count needs NumPy 2.0 or later; pq_scratch.py falls back to np.unpackbits on older versions.
PQ does poorly on these 64-dimensional vectors because much of their spread is random noise, which nothing compresses well. Measure on your own embeddings before choosing a scheme.

modules.title: Hybrid search, filtering and evaluation
modules.summary: Measure relevance with labelled queries, combine BM25 with dense retrieval and tune the fusion without fooling yourself, and filter vector search without losing results.

lessons.title: Evaluating relevance with labelled queries
objectives: Build a labelled query set with graded relevance
Calculate recall@k, MRR and nDCG, and judge whether a difference is real
key_points: Relevance evaluation needs queries like real users' and judgements of which documents answer them (qrels), ideally graded, such as 2 for an answer and 1 for related. Take queries from search logs where you can, and label them without seeing which system found what.

recall@k is the share of a query's relevant documents in the top k; MRR averages 1/rank of the first relevant result; nDCG@k sums gains (2^grade − 1) divided by log2(rank + 1) and scales by the best possible ordering, rewarding the most relevant documents first.
Split the queries: tune weights, thresholds and model choices on a dev set and report the test set once, at the end. Tuning on the queries you report gives optimistic numbers.

Small query sets are noisy. Compare two systems query by query and bootstrap over queries for an interval on the difference: in the lab, a hybrid's nDCG@10 gain of 0.004 over dense retrieval on 20 test queries had an interval of +0.000 to +0.011.
Read the failures, not just the averages: list the queries where systems disagree, because they show what each retriever misses, such as exact codes for dense models and paraphrases for BM25.

lessons.title: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense results
objectives: Explain what lexical and dense retrieval each do well
Fuse two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted combination of scores
key_points: BM25 scores documents by the query's words that they contain, weighted by rarity (IDF), with saturation through k1 and length normalisation through b. It excels at identifiers, error codes and rare names, which dense models often blur.

Dense retrieval matches meaning across different words, such as "I'm off sick today" to an article on reporting sickness absence. In the lab it beat BM25 on recall@5 (0.900 against 0.725), yet only BM25 found the article searched for by its ID.

Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 / (k + rank) from each list, with k = 60 by convention. It needs no score calibration but weights both retrievers equally, so a much weaker one drags results down: in the lab, RRF scored nDCG@10 0.785 against 0.924 for dense alone.

A convex combination, w × dense + (1 − w) × BM25 after min-max normalising each query's scores, lets the weight reflect each retriever's strength. Choose w on dev queries (the lab chose 0.9) and confirm on test.

In production, take the top 100 or so from each retriever, fuse the union and re-rank if needed. Learned sparse models such as SPLADE, and the hybrid queries built into several vector databases, are other ways to get both behaviours.

lessons.title: Filtering vector search
objectives: Compare post-filtering, pre-filtering and filtering during the search
Choose a filtering strategy from how selective the filter is
key_points: Post-filtering takes the index's top k and drops rows that fail the filter, so a filter matching 5% of rows leaves about 0.5 of 10 results. Over-fetching helps only partly, because the factor needed grows as the filter narrows.

Pre-filtering finds the matching rows first, for example with a B-tree index, and searches only them, exactly: perfect recall, and cheap when few rows match, which makes it the right plan for highly selective filters.

Filtering during the search skips non-matching vectors as the index is traversed. It works for broad filters, but with very selective ones IVF's probed lists hold few matches and HNSW's graph falls apart: in the lab, HNSW found 4.2 of 10 results for a 0.5% tenant.

Engines combine the strategies: several estimate how many rows match and switch to an exact scan of them when there are few, and pgvector 0.8.0 and later can keep scanning an HNSW index until enough rows pass the filter (iterative index scans).

Partition when a filter is always present, such as one tenant per query: an index or partition per tenant keeps searches small and customers' data apart. Enforce access rules in the filter itself, never by trusting a later step to drop documents.

"""Module 4 lab: BM25, dense and hybrid retrieval over the help-centre articles. Fusion is tuned on the dev
queries and scored once on the test queries with recall@5, MRR@10 and nDCG@10."""
import argparse

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--dense", choices=["minilm", "lsa"], default="minilm")
a = p.parse_args()

docs, qs = pd.read_csv("data/helpdesk.csv"), pd.read_csv("data/queries.csv")
text = (docs["id"] + " " + docs["title"] + ". " + docs["body"]).tolist()
ids = docs["id"].to_numpy()

# ---- BM25 from term counts (k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75)
cv = CountVectorizer()                                   # tokens: runs of two or more letters or digits
tf = cv.fit_transform(text).toarray().astype(float)      # documents x terms
n_docs = len(text)
df = (tf > 0).sum(axis=0)
idf = np.log(1 + (n_docs - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5))
dl = tf.sum(axis=1)


def bm25(query, k1=1.2, b=0.75):
    cols = [cv.vocabulary_[t] for t in cv.build_analyzer()(query) if t in cv.vocabulary_]
    f = tf[:, cols]
    return (idf[cols] * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl[:, None] / dl.mean()))).sum(axis=1)


lexical = np.stack([bm25(q) for q in qs["query"]])

# ---- dense: a small pretrained model, or LSA if you can't download one
if a.dense == "minilm":
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
    model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
    D = model.encode(text, normalize_embeddings=True)
    Q = model.encode(qs["query"].tolist(), normalize_embeddings=True)
else:
    from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
    from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
    from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize
    tv = TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True).fit(text)
    svd = TruncatedSVD(40, random_state=0).fit(tv.transform(text))
    D = normalize(svd.transform(tv.transform(text)))
    Q = normalize(svd.transform(tv.transform(qs["query"])))
dense = Q @ D.T


# ---- fusion
def ranks(s):
    return np.argsort(np.argsort(-s, axis=1, kind="stable"), axis=1) + 1   # 1 = best


def rrf(*runs, k=60):
    return sum(1.0 / (k + ranks(s)) for s in runs)


def minmax(s):
    lo, hi = s.min(axis=1, keepdims=True), s.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return (s - lo) / np.where(hi > lo, hi - lo, 1.0)


def convex(w):
    return w * minmax(dense) + (1 - w) * minmax(lexical)


# ---- metrics, per query
gains = [{d: int(g) for d, g in (x.split(":") for x in r.split(";"))} for r in qs["relevant"]]


def per_query(scores):
    out = []
    for s, g in zip(scores, gains):
        top = ids[np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")][:10]
        recall5 = len(set(g) & set(top[:5])) / len(g)
        first = next((i for i, d in enumerate(top) if d in g), None)
        rr = 0.0 if first is None else 1.0 / (first + 1)
        dcg = sum((2 ** g.get(d, 0) - 1) / np.log2(i + 2) for i, d in enumerate(top))
        idcg = sum((2 ** v - 1) / np.log2(i + 2) for i, v in enumerate(sorted(g.values(), reverse=True)))
        out.append((recall5, rr, dcg / idcg))
    return np.array(out)


dev, test = (qs["split"] == "dev").to_numpy(), (qs["split"] == "test").to_numpy()
best_w = max(np.round(np.arange(0, 1.01, 0.1), 1), key=lambda w: per_query(convex(w))[dev, 2].mean())
print(f"dense model: {a.dense}; convex weight on dense chosen on dev queries: w = {best_w}")
runs = {"BM25": lexical, "dense": dense, "RRF (k=60)": rrf(lexical, dense), f"convex w={best_w}": convex(best_w)}
print(f"{'test queries':<16}{'recall@5':>9}{'MRR@10':>8}{'nDCG@10':>9}")
results = {name: per_query(s) for name, s in runs.items()}
for name, r in results.items():
    print(f"{name:<16}" + "".join(f"{v:>9.3f}" if i != 1 else f"{v:>8.3f}" for i, v in enumerate(r[test].mean(0))))

# ---- where the two retrievers disagree
first_hit = {name: [ids[np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")][0] in g for s, g in zip(sc, gains)]
             for name, sc in [("BM25", lexical), ("dense", dense)]}
for q, b, dn in zip(qs["query"][test], np.array(first_hit["BM25"])[test], np.array(first_hit["dense"])[test]):
    if b != dn:
        print(f"  only {'BM25' if b else 'dense'} ranks a relevant article first: {q!r}")

# ---- is the hybrid's gain over dense real? a paired bootstrap over the 20 test queries
diff = results[f"convex w={best_w}"][test, 2] - results["dense"][test, 2]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
boot = [rng.choice(diff, size=len(diff)).mean() for _ in range(2000)]
lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"nDCG@10 gain of the convex hybrid over dense: {diff.mean():+.3f} (95% bootstrap interval {lo:+.3f} to {hi:+.3f})")

"""Module 4 lab, part 2: filtered vector search. Find each query's 10 nearest vectors within one tenant,
by post-filtering, by pre-filtering, and with the filter applied inside FAISS's IVF and HNSW searches."""
import faiss
import numpy as np

from vecs import load, recall_at_k, top_k

faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1)
base, queries = load()
tenant = np.load("data/tenant.npy")
n, d = base.shape
k = 10

ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), d, 256, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
ivf.train(base)
ivf.add(base)
hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 16, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
hnsw.hnsw.efConstruction = 80
hnsw.add(base)
scores = queries @ base.T                                   # exact scores, for the reference answers


def returned(found):
    return np.mean([(row >= 0).sum() for row in found])     # FAISS pads missing results with -1


print(f"{'tenant':<7}{'share':>6} | {'post k=10':>9} {'post k=100':>10} | {'IVF':>11} {'HNSW ef=64':>11}")
for t in [0, 2, 4, 6, 7]:
    ids = np.flatnonzero(tenant == t)
    truth = ids[top_k(scores[:, ids], k)]                    # pre-filter: exact search inside the tenant
    post10 = [[i for i in row if tenant[i] == t][:k] for row in top_k(scores, 10)]
    post100 = [[i for i in row if tenant[i] == t][:k] for row in top_k(scores, 100)]
    sel = faiss.IDSelectorBatch(ids.astype(np.int64))
    _, f_ivf = ivf.search(queries, k, params=faiss.SearchParametersIVF(sel=sel, nprobe=16))
    _, f_hnsw = hnsw.search(queries, k, params=faiss.SearchParametersHNSW(sel=sel, efSearch=64))
    print(f"{t:<7}{len(ids) / n:>6.1%} | {np.mean([len(r) for r in post10]):>9.1f} "
          f"{np.mean([len(r) for r in post100]):>10.1f} | {returned(f_ivf):>4.1f} r={recall_at_k(f_ivf, truth):.2f} "
          f"{returned(f_hnsw):>4.1f} r={recall_at_k(f_hnsw, truth):.2f}")
print("post columns: results left after filtering the top 10 or top 100; IVF and HNSW: results returned, "
      "and recall against the pre-filtered exact answer")

modules.title: Vector databases in production
modules.summary: Choose between a library, a PostgreSQL extension and a dedicated vector database, run vector search inside PostgreSQL with pgvector, and operate an index through updates, model changes and growth.

lessons.title: Choosing a vector store
objectives: Compare vector libraries, database extensions and dedicated vector databases
Choose a vector store for a workload from its requirements
key_points: FAISS is a library: it runs inside your process with the widest choice of index types and GPU support, but persistence, metadata, filtering beyond ID selectors, replication and an API are yours to build. It suits batch jobs, research and services you control end to end.

pgvector adds a vector type and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes to PostgreSQL, so vectors sit beside the rows they describe, with the transactions, joins, backups and replication you already run; its scale is that of your PostgreSQL deployment.

Dedicated vector databases are servers built around vector search: Qdrant (written in Rust) filters on JSON payloads during its HNSW search, Weaviate (in Go) has built-in hybrid BM25 and vector queries, and Milvus is built for distributed scale with many index types.

Compare candidates on what your workload needs: index types and quantisation, behaviour with selective filters, hybrid search, updates and deletes, multi-tenancy, consistency after writes, replication and sharding, and the operations work each adds.

Benchmark on your own vectors, filters and query mix at your target recall. Published benchmarks use other data, settings and hardware, and features change quickly, so check current documentation for the versions you'll run.

lessons.title: Vector search in PostgreSQL with pgvector
objectives: Store and query vectors with pgvector's types, operators and indexes
Tune and inspect pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat indexes
key_points: pgvector stores vectors in a vector(n) column and compares them with operators: <-> for L2 distance, <#> for the negative inner product (negated so that ascending order puts the best first) and <=> for cosine distance. A query orders by the operator and takes a LIMIT.

An index serves one operator, chosen by its operator class: USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) serves <=>. WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64) are pgvector's defaults; check with EXPLAIN that queries use the index.

At query time, SET hnsw.ef_search (default 40) trades recall for speed. IVFFlat takes lists when it's built and ivfflat.probes (default 1) at query time, and should be built once the table has data, because its lists come from k-means on the rows present.

WHERE conditions are applied to the rows the approximate index returns, so a selective filter can leave few results. pgvector 0.8.0 added iterative index scans (SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order), which keep scanning until enough rows match.

HNSW builds are fastest when the graph fits in maintenance_work_mem, and parallel builds use shared memory: in a Docker container, raise --shm-size, or the build can fail with 'could not resize shared memory segment'.
Indexed vector columns are limited to 2,000 dimensions. The halfvec type (float16) indexes up to 4,000 and halves storage, and the bit and sparsevec types cover binary and sparse vectors.

lessons.title: Operating a vector index
objectives: Plan ingestion, updates and deletes for a vector index
Re-index safely when the embedding model changes, and monitor search quality
key_points: Ingest idempotently: give every chunk a stable ID derived from its document and position, upsert in batches, and record the source version and the embedding model, so that reruns never create duplicates.

Updates and deletes are cheap to request but costly to absorb: HNSW indexes and many databases mark deleted vectors and skip them until compaction or a rebuild, so track the share of deleted entries and plan regular rebuilds.

A new embedding model means a new index: build it beside the old one from the same documents, compare both on the labelled queries, switch reads with an alias or a configuration change, and keep the old index until the new one has proved itself.

Monitor search like any service, with latency percentiles, errors, index size and memory, plus a canary set of queries with known exact neighbours whose recall you recompute after every change and on a schedule.

Plan growth from bytes per vector. When one machine's memory runs out, shard by ID (each query then searches every shard) or by tenant (only its tenant's shard), and add replicas for throughput and availability.

"""Module 5 lab: write the unit-length collection and the first 100 queries as CSV files PostgreSQL can load."""
import numpy as np

from vecs import load

base, queries = load()
tenant = np.load("data/tenant.npy")


def literal(v):
    return "[" + ",".join(f"{x:.6g}" for x in v) + "]"          # pgvector's text format: [1,2,3]


with open("data/pg_items.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("id,tenant,embedding\n")
    for i, (t, v) in enumerate(zip(tenant, base)):
        f.write(f'{i},{t},"{literal(v)}"\n')
with open("data/pg_queries.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("id,embedding\n")
    for i, v in enumerate(queries[:100]):
        f.write(f'{i},"{literal(v)}"\n')
print(f"wrote data/pg_items.csv ({len(base)} rows) and data/pg_queries.csv (100 rows)")

hints: If CREATE INDEX fails with 'could not resize shared memory segment', the container's /dev/shm is too small: recreate it with --shm-size=512m, or SET max_parallel_maintenance_workers = 0 before building.
Recall can differ by a point or two from build to build: HNSW draws each vector's layers at random, and parallel builds insert in varying order. Look at the trend, not the third decimal.
Docker Hub can rate-limit anonymous pulls: sign in with docker login, or wait and retry.
To connect from Python (for example with psycopg), add -p 5432:5432 to docker run; this lab runs psql inside the container, so it doesn't need the port.

project.title: Build and evaluate a semantic search service
project.brief: A support organisation wants semantic search over its knowledge base, for staff today and as the retrieval layer of an AI assistant later. Build it on the course's help-centre articles, extended to at least 300 articles of your own writing or from an openly licensed source, or on a document set you're allowed to use, with at least 40 labelled queries split into dev and test. Choose and justify an embedding model. Build exact, IVF or HNSW and one compressed index, and pick a configuration that meets recall@10 of 0.95 against exact search within a memory budget you state. Add BM25 and a fusion tuned on dev queries only. Enforce an audience filter (all staff, managers, IT) so that nobody sees articles they shouldn't, with filtered queries still returning k results. Serve it from FAISS or pgvector, and plan how to re-index when the embedding model changes.
deliverables: The code: ingestion with stable IDs, embedding, index builds, search with filters and fusion, and the evaluation scripts
An index report: recall@10 against exact search, latency percentiles and bytes per vector for every configuration tried, and the one chosen for the budget
A relevance report on the test queries: recall@5, MRR@10 and nDCG@10 for BM25, dense and the hybrid, a bootstrap interval for the main comparison, and the disagreements analysed
A filtering test showing that no query returns an article outside the user's audience and that filtered queries still return k results
A one-page vector store decision comparing FAISS, pgvector and one dedicated vector database for this workload
A runbook: adding and deleting articles, rebuilding the index, switching embedding models, and the recall canary
